title: Measuring and Charging for Retained Context in Long-Context LLM Services
authors: Yi Lu, Qianshi Lin, Yumeng Yang et al.
abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) services charge for repeated context, yet billing weights need not reflect its contribution to answer quality. We present a three-layer framework separating content relevance, observable proxies and auditable positional weights. Context-ablation experiments show that relevance dominates position and that distance-decay families do not outperform a relevance-only baseline. A measured serving stack shows that cache hits reduce repeated-prefix compute cost by

title: Grading Executable Legal Rules Against Independent Records: Transitional Provisions and Korean SME Status
authors: Jinhyung Bae
abstract: Laws are increasingly turned into programs that decide cases, such as whether a firm was a small or medium enterprise (SME) on a given date, and large language models (LLMs) now write them. The programs are usually graded against answers written by someone who read the same law, so a program can score well by sharing the grader's reading rather than by getting the law right. LexTemporis grades them instead against records of what actually happened: 10,901 firm-years of SME status disclosed by Ko

title: A Mechanistic Analysis of In-Context Learning and Out-of-Context Hallucination
authors: Tianxiang Chen, Jingyuan Zhou, Guoyao Yang et al.
abstract: Large language models can infer and follow specific rules through in-context learning (ICL), yet may fail to remain faithful to provided evidence, giving rise to out-of-context (OOC) hallucination. Existing work has largely investigated the underlying mechanisms of ICL and OOC hallucination along separate lines. However, this separation obscures the mechanistic basis for these seemingly opposing outcomes. In this work, we study this contrast through the unified view of functional roles in dynami

title: Dual-Manifold Variational Autoencoders
authors: Hongxu Chen, Chun Wang, Yanghao Wang et al.
abstract: In latent diffusion models, expanding the latent dimension of variational autoencoders (VAEs) is essential to push the upper bound of reconstruction quality. However, without explicit structural constraints, such unregularized expansion easily yields a rugged and ill-conditioned latent manifold, causing generated latents to drift off the manifold during generation (i.e., off-manifold problem). Recent works smooth this manifold by using external foundation models (e.g., DINOv2) as a topological r

title: A Hierarchical Onboard Vision-Language-Navigation Framework for Aerial Robots in Complex Environments
authors: Yuze Wu, Mo Zhu, Xingxing Li et al.
abstract: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are expected to achieve semantic reasoning, intelligent decision-making, and long-horizon navigation under strict onboard constraints. While recent foundation-model-driven approaches have shown promising progress toward this goal, existing methods remain limited by challenges in 3D data availability, trajectory feasibility, long-horizon reasoning, and computational efficiency in complex environments. To bridge these gaps, we propose VLN-AR, a hierarchical vision-l

title: Cardiac MRI-informed electrocardiography enables biologically grounded cardiomyopathy detection
authors: Zhengyao Ding, Kewen Wang, Yujian Hu et al.
abstract: Precise myocardial phenotyping at population scale is limited by the cost and accessibility of cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), whereas electrocardiography (ECG) is widely available but reflects electrical rather than structural and functional information. Here we develop MyoECG, a cross-modal representation learning framework that distils myocardial structural and functional knowledge from CMR into standard 12-lead ECGs, enabling imaging-informed cardiomyopathy detection and subtype classifica

title: Vanguard: Knowing When to Trust the Draft in Speculative Vision-Language Agents
authors: Hanqi Mao, Jiajun Fan, Ruihan Guo et al.
abstract: Vision-language agents that browse websites, operate phones and act in homes reason before every action, so every step waits for a large model, a latency and cost that stand in the way of deployment. Step-level speculation lets a small model draft each step and calls the large model only on rejected drafts, but its outcome rests on the judge, and a judge that reads only a step's text cannot tell whether the step fits the screen it acts on. We find that a few samples of a small model can contain

title: Asking but Missing: Decision Coverage in Natural-Language Data Querying
authors: Hangle Hu, Chenyu Hou, Bin Cao et al.
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to translate natural language questions about structured data into executable programs. A fundamental challenge is recognizing when a question admits multiple computational interpretations and identifying the decisions needed to resolve them. We investigate whether language models recognize these unresolved decisions before generating code, or silently adopt assumptions that may lead to incorrect results. We refer to the latter behavior as Underspecifi

title: NarrowSpec: Draft Hidden Width Need Not Match the Target in Speculative Decoding
authors: Alagappan Valliappan, Ankit More, Dheevatsa Mudigere et al.
abstract: Speculative decoding is widely used to speed up generation in large language models (LLMs), with a small draft model proposing tokens that one forward pass of the target model verifies. Draft models that read the target's hidden states, such as DFlash and EAGLE-3, typically inherit the target's hidden width. We show that the draft's whole residual stream can run at half or a quarter of that width while largely preserving acceptance. For DFlash, which borrows the target's vocabulary projection, t

title: Reliability is a user-specific property of large language models
authors: Xingyu Zhao
abstract: Public benchmarks support comparisons of large language model (LLM) capabilities, yet users can experience the same highly ranked model differently. Drawing on traditional software reliability, we argue that the reliability of an LLM service should be assessed for specified users and conditions of use. This requires more than a capability score: evaluation evidence must support a claim about failure during future operation. We distinguish testing to discover faults from testing to assess reliabi

title: Localizing Text Anonymization for Trustworthy AI: Extending RAT-Bench to Malaysian Microdata and PII
authors: David Hong Liang Chew, Zexi Yao, Nataša Krčo et al.
abstract: As governments and organizations adopt foundation models for public services and workplace productivity, sensitive citizen, employee, and administrative text may enter LLM workflows through inference, retrieval, fine-tuning, or local model development. We examine whether text anonymizers transfer to new deployment settings by extending RAT-Bench to Malaysia using local microdata, Malaysian PII formats, and culturally grounded transcripts in Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia. We evaluate NER-

title: KnowMe Paper Radar: Lightweight Discovery of Promising Papers in the Age of Autoresearch
authors: Zhuo Chen, Jian Wang, Jinjie Gu et al.
abstract: The growing volume of topically similar papers makes it difficult to identify new work that can offer useful research insights or methodological guidance. We present KnowMe Paper Radar, a lightweight discovery tool that combines multiple sources of evidence into personalized reading priorities. Users specify topics, priorities, exclusions and dates; the system brings together topical relevance, recency, author research histories, collaboration paths and direction-specific institutional context.

title: Structured Extraction of Diffraction Data from Covalent Organic Frameworks
authors: Shenghan Gao, Zhiling Zheng
abstract: Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) is the primary structural evidence for covalent organic frameworks (COFs) and many other materials. Yet decades of measured patterns exist only as images in published figures. Automatic recovery is difficult, because PXRD figures vary widely in format, from a single curve to crowded stacks with labels, insets, and neighboring plots that challenge traditional computer vision. This work presents a pipeline in which a vision large language model (LLM) interprets the

title: Searching the Pareto Front: Multi-Objective Retrieval for Heterogeneous Scientific Modalities
authors: Song Young Oh, Nesar Ramachandra, Bin Xia et al.
abstract: In cosmology, surveys span different sky regions and wavelength ranges, resulting in uneven modality coverage across observational datasets. Such heterogeneity can be addressed through either multimodal foundation models (FMs), which learn shared embedding spaces, or independently learned modality embeddings combined via late fusion. We investigate whether the latter provides an adaptive alternative to FM-based scientific retrieval. We evaluate this approach on a galaxy retrieval task spanning d

title: MKA: Evaluating Multimodal Knowledge Agents on end-to-end professional tasks
authors: Anima Singh, Suhas Yogin, Weicheng Kuo et al.
abstract: We introduce the Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark, which measures how well autonomous agents perform end-to-end professional knowledge work that depends on visual understanding. Each task requires an agent to extract and combine information from multiple visually dense files, such as CAD blueprints, electronics schematics, radiographs, complex charts and geospatial maps, and to produce a standalone deliverable in .xlsx, .pptx, .pdf, .docx, .html or .png format. Existing benchmarks leav

title: EverydayBench: Evaluating Satisfactory Completion of Live User-Facing Digital Work
authors: Fangrui Huang, Bingyang Wang, Chuhan Li et al.
abstract: Everyday digital tasks, from selecting products and planning trips to conducting research and creating artifacts, require AI agents to deliver useful outcomes rather than merely retrieve web information. Yet evaluating these outcomes on the live web is challenging, as a single request may admit multiple valid results, and changing web information can alter which results remain valid over time. Although existing benchmarks address aspects of this setting, they do not fully integrate predefined su

title: Resolution as Attention for Efficient Agent Memory Perception
authors: Siqi Xiang, Zhipeng Xu, Shengrui Liu et al.
abstract: LLM-based agents accumulate extensive interaction histories when solving complex, long-horizon tasks, making efficient memory management critical to their performance and scalability. While existing memory management methods primarily focus on what to retain or retrieve, they often overlook how much perceptual detail should be allocated to individual past interactions. We posit that effective agent memory depends not only on the information preserved, but also on the granularity at which each pa

title: 3D GameDev Arena: Benchmarking Coding Agents That Plan, Build, and Playtest extreme Long-Horizon Browser Games
authors: Bizhe Bai, Jiliang Jian, Yuqing Yan et al.
abstract: Coding agents now resolve repository issues and generate compact playable games, but whether they can build a large 3D game from scratch remains open. Such games tightly couple mechanics, scenes, assets, and interaction logic, and their quality rests on player enjoyment, which existing benchmarks rarely assess. Thus, we introduce 3D GameDev Arena, a first extreme long-horizon benchmark of 108 from-scratch game-development tasks across 14 genres. Given only a text specification and UI/UX referenc

title: Can you make models believe false facts in the prompt?
authors: Ananya Sutradhar, Fabien Roger
abstract: Making LLMs believe false facts is useful for alignment evaluations and for building model organisms. Previous work explored doing so with Synthetic Document Finetuning (SDF). But SDF requires fine-tuning one new model for each set of injected false beliefs. To enable larger scale SDF-powered alignment evaluations, we attempt to produce a single model that believes any fact placed in a <facts> tag in the prompt. To do so, we explore doing prompt-conditioned SDF: fine-tuning a model on synt

title: Evidence-Based Credit Assignment for Search-Augmented Language Models
authors: Wen Wang, Jindong Wang, Jiahua Bao et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning from terminal answer rewards enables search-augmented language models to interleave reasoning and retrieval without step-level annotations, yet outcome supervision assigns identical credit to every search in a trajectory regardless of whether it retrieved useful information. This limitation is especially severe when all sampled rollouts for a question fail, collapsing group-centered outcome advantages to zero even when trajectories gather markedly different evidence. title: Toaster: Nonlinear Memory from Cascaded Linear Memories and Target Propagation
authors: Zeman Li, Ali Behrouz, Yuan Deng et al.
abstract: Recurrent memories let language models process long sequences with a fixed-size state. Linear memories such as DeltaNet and KDA store one matrix and take one delta-rule step per token. The product of a chunk of such steps has an exact WY form, so they train fast. Deep memories such as TTT-MLP and Titans store a small MLP, which can hold maps that no matrix can, but their update has no WY form. Toaster bridges the two by building on a known fact: a gradient step on a linear layer is a delta-rule

title: Auditable Clinical Support with Decision Agents
authors: Tiancheng Bao, Riga Wu, Jan Wienhold et al.
abstract: Emergency care requires auditable decisions, but a language-model agent just outputs text. We introduce Decision2Care, a decision agent that generates a probability for every option at each step. It diagnosed 546 emergency admissions across 12 diseases with 86.5% accuracy in a median of 2.2 s; language-model agents reached 86.1 to 91.7% but took more than 90 s. Its drug orders were judged guideline-adherent more often than documented first-day care and with about half as many records, it predict

title: StringQFT: A Multiuse Textbook Resource for AI-Assisted Theoretical Physics
authors: Xingyang Yu
abstract: We present StringQFT as a textbook collection for string constructions of quantum field theory and as infrastructure for AI-assisted theoretical physics. The collection comprises 18 volumes, 190 chapters and 3,795 pages, covering brane probes, brane webs, geometric engineering, F-theory constructions, wrapped M5-branes and exact worldsheet constructions. Its open-book benchmark inventory contains 1,073 items, including 499 with automatic finite-answer checking. For retrieval-augmented generation

title: RagHarnessDebugger: Jev-Guided Agentic RAG in Contract Inference Repair Auditing
authors: Moriya Dechtiar, Daniel Martin Katz, Michael J. Bommarito et al.
abstract: Agentic systems using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) must repair their own answers by gathering more evidence, testing alternative policies and deciding if, when, and what repairs are needed. Yet how do we know if a system's repairs are working when metrics like accuracy can be misleading? We present RagHarnessDebugger, a framework that records every repair decision in a Jev-guided harness for contract inference and audits the record to facilitate complete debugging of all decisions taken

title: StitchRAG: Constructing Compact and Evidence-Preserving Contexts for RAG with Diffusion-Based Stitching
authors: Minsang Kim, Junpyo Lim, Heeje Cho et al.
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves factuality by grounding large language models (LLMs) in external evidence. However, long retrieved contexts incur computational overhead and can even hurt performance due to noisy or irrelevant content. We propose \textsc{StitchRAG}, a framework for constructing compact context in RAG. \textsc{StitchRAG} builds a faithful, information-dense context while dynamically compressing the retrieved passages. We adapt the size reduction ratio to each passage

title: NONSENSE: Non-Semantic Strings Expose Semanticity Gaps in Dense Retrieval
authors: Ankit Gupta
abstract: Dense retrieval is central to modern search, question answering, and retrieval-augmented generation, where high similarity is often treated as evidence of semantic relevance. We examine how far this assumption can be stressed. NONSENSE is a black-box sparse-edit probe that constructs visibly non-semantic strings while forbidding query-term copying, optimizing only the dense similarity between a query and the string. Across five BEIR-style datasets and three popular single-vector retrievers, thes

title: RAG in a Trenchcoat: When Minimal Memory Is Enough for Agentic Systems, and When It Isn't
authors: Jingyu Liu, Zongze Li, Zach Xu et al.
abstract: Agentic memory research has accumulated extraction, supersession, reflection, and graph synthesis on top of retrieval-augmented generation. However, we found that almost none of those primitives earn their cost in our tested memory benchmarks: we show this with BRIDGE, a deliberately minimal RAG memory with chained observation notes, hybrid BM25 with cosine retrieval, and chronological rendering, which reaches parity within bootstrap CI with the prior SOTA on LongMemEval-S and BEAM, and beats th

title: MANGO Arena: Same Seeds, Different Chains Evaluating LLM Agents in a Disrupted Supply Chain
authors: Sara Amar
abstract: We introduce MANGO Arena, an open-source testbed in which four LLM agents each run one company in a serial supply chain adapted from MANGO, a classroom factory-management game. The environment enforces hard rules (a truck limit, a no-credit cash constraint and production capacity), logs every blocked attempt to break them, and gives agents a public message board on which side payments are explicitly forbidden. This lets one environment measure three things at once: an economic outcome (the bullw

title: ARISE: Practical Self-Evolving Memory for Accurate and Cost-Efficient Enterprise Agents
authors: Jiangyun Zhang, Zhou Tang, Kristen Surrao et al.
abstract: Enterprise LLM agents operate in dynamic environments where foundation models evolve rapidly, workflows update frequently, and deployments need to satisfy accuracy and cost requirements. We propose ARISE (Agent Refinement through Iterative Self-Evaluation), a practical memory architecture in which the agent's memory evolves from its own failures without updating model weights, tools, or workflow logic. ARISE uses the model itself or a teacher model to attribute the failures and propose correctio

title: Safe to Omit, Worth Omitting? Keeping the Answer and Cutting Latency When an LLM Agent Skips Another's Message
authors: Xinyang Li, Chih-Hsuan Yang, Xiaolong Ma et al.
abstract: In multi-agent systems, a receiver agent often waits for a helper agent's message (text or its latent KV cache), which can improve performance but adds latency. We study when a receiver agent can skip the message safely (the final answer rarely changes) and beneficially (the time saved exceeds the cost of deciding). title: LProp: Propagating Latent Uncertainty through Evidence-Conditioned Belief Revision in LLM Agents
authors: Kaiwen Shi, Zheyuan Zhang, Weixiang Sun et al.
abstract: When LLM agents pass intermediate judgments downstream without uncertainty, later decisions may treat tentative assumptions as facts. Effective uncertainty propagation must preserve information for correction and update inherited beliefs as new evidence arrives. Yet scalar scores omit information needed for revision, while detailed descriptions and reflection incur additional costs. We introduce Latent Uncertainty, a latent-space estimator that preserves uncertainty-relevant information without

title: SpecLook: Speculating Where to Look for Fast and Reliable Agentic MLLMs
authors: Xi Ding, Jiawei Zhang
abstract: Agentic multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that think with images interleave reasoning with zoom-in tool calls. However, this sequential loop is slow, and its answers carry no reliability score. Prior speculation of tokens, reasoning steps, or answers keeps the loop, and answer speculation also accepts confident errors. title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Navigation Behavior of Vision-Language Model Agents Reading Emergency CT and MRI Examinations
authors: Jonathan Lichtle, Aymen Meddeb, Antonin Birot et al.
abstract: Purpose. To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and image navigation behavior of vision-language model (VLM) agents under varying exploration strategies. Materials and Methods. In this retrospective study, six VLMs read 100 emergency CT and MRI examinations published in a public archive (March 2025-August 2026) under four conditions (free navigation, navigation from a key slice, and all slices or key slices in a single request), twice each (4800 runs). Nine radiologists read 30 of those cases. A la

title: Reliability by Architecture: Agentic Workflows for Validated Multi-Physics Simulation from Natural Language
authors: Søren Taverniers, Eric Darve, Hamdi A. Tchelepi
abstract: Preparing, executing, and validating strongly coupled multi-physics simulations require expert time. Agentic workflows use large language models (LLMs) to coordinate them from natural-language descriptions, but reliability requires checks of physical consistency and fidelity to the problem description. Our agentic harness implements explicit task allocation: LLMs interpret user requests and simulator diagnostics, generate input components not covered by predefined construction rules, and propose

title: Tracking Representations in LLM Reasoning Traces for Iterated Games
authors: Chaipat Tirapongprasert, Rajarshi Das, Parijat Dube
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents achieve state-of-the-art performance across domains through chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. Despite their ubiquitous use, little is understood about the relationship between the externalized trace and the model's actual computation. We address this by investigating how LLM agents make decisions in iterative games with incomplete information. Using a series of mechanistic interpretability techniques, we find that the model forms and iteratively revises an inter

title: QDA: Closed-Loop LLM Quantization Design with Agents
authors: Xingyang Li, Tianlang Zhao, Song Han et al.
abstract: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds lead to better recipes. However, evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes t

title: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve?
authors: Shobhita Sundaram, Cansu Sancaktar, Phillip Isola
abstract: LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for contex

title: Dynamic Task Allocation with Dialogue
authors: Matthew Groholski, Weiwei Gu, Nakul Gopalan
abstract: Effective multi-agent collaboration requires agents to adapt task allocation as goals and responsibilities evolve. Prior task-allocation frameworks often assume static goals, full observability, or rely on large language models (LLMs) without explicit, verifiable beliefs about task allocation or intent. These assumptions limit their applicability to real-world collaboration, where agents often lack full information about each other's actions, progress, or local environment. To support dynamic ta

title: ForecastGym: A Live, Controlled, and Replayable Benchmark for Forecasting Agents
authors: Yicheng Tao, Yuante Li, Zipei Fan
abstract: Agents built on large language models (LLMs) increasingly forecast real-world events by searching the Web and reasoning over what they find. How well such an agent forecasts depends on both the retrieved evidence and the model, making control over that evidence essential for evaluation. Live evaluations can mix retrieval with reasoning when each system searches on its own, while retrospective search can leak later information through date filters or today's ranking of historical pages. Comparing

title: Stopping Is Not the Limit: Understanding and Eliciting Agent Capability in Long-Horizon Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Deokhyung Kang, Minjae Gwon, Sangdon Park
abstract: Vulnerability exploitation tests whether language model agents can develop working exploits from known software flaws. Sequential test-time scaling can improve exploitation performance, but larger budgets do not ensure sustained exploration: agents often stop with budget remaining. Yet what happens when execution continues beyond stopping remains underexplored. We investigate this gap on ExploitBench using DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and MiMo-V2.6-Pro. We find additional verified gains after the firs

title: Idempotency Is Not Recovery: A Fault-Injection Study of Language-Model Agent Tool Actions
authors: Song Xu
abstract: When a language-model agent's tool call is interrupted, the action may already have changed an external system without confirmation. Retrying risks duplication; assuming success may conceal an action that never occurred. We study these failure modes in a controlled agent runtime combining authorization, an action ledger, target-side idempotency, reconciliation, and evidence sealing. We inject ten single-host fault classes and compare four configurations and three ablations using a target-side or

title: EvoSkill-S1: Evolving Reusable Skills with Genetic-Inspired Operators
authors: Yujun Wang, Jiqiang Li, Yinuo Lu et al.
abstract: Reusable skills allow language-model agents to accumulate and reuse problem-solving experience. However, most existing methods improve a skill bank only indirectly through rollout-driven accumulation and heuristic reflection, often resulting in shallow and weakly controlled updates. We present EvoSkill-S1, an RL-driven framework that instead treats reusable skills themselves as the direct objects of evolution. Given hard-negative failures, EvoSkill-S1 selects parent skills and transforms them in

title: Evolution Under Fire: Evolving Agent Safety Harnesses with Adaptive Injection Stressors
authors: Yujun Wang, Yilun Liu, Jinhe Bi et al.
abstract: Tool-using language-model agents must act on information from untrusted emails, webpages, and documents. This creates a central security challenge: malicious instructions and legitimate task directives can arrive through the same interaction channel. Existing defenses are largely hand-designed and static, making further improvements dependent on repeated manual redesign. We introduce Evolution Under Fire, a staged framework that couples safety-harness evolution with adaptive stressor evolution.

title: JET: Just-Enough Exploration Tuning for Efficient Tool-Calling Agents in Repository-Level Question Answering
authors: Yoonho Choi, Taehyeon Han, Seonghyeon Lee
abstract: In repository-level question answering (QA), an agent explores a code repository with tools and should answer a question once enough information is gathered. Nevertheless, we find that LLM agents often continue to invoke tools even after the gathered information is already sufficient to answer. We call this phenomenon over-exploration. Moreover, even though existing methods improve task performance through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories, SFT also propagates the over-explorat

title: LMLineage: Content Lineage and Context Governance for LLM Agents
authors: Wei Hou, Jingxin Geng, Xin Chen et al.
abstract: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift mic

title: Think Once, Act Fast: Cost-Effective Recursive Self-Improvement for Decision Model Harness
authors: Siqi Lai, Haitao Li, Hao Liu
abstract: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selecti

title: LMMR: Learned Multigranular Memory Retrieval for Small Language Model Agents
authors: Pengfeng Song, Yunkai Zhuang, Liye Shi
abstract: Small language model agents have limited space to read the memory needed for multi-hop questions. Relevant facts are often scattered across records whose surrounding text consumes much of that space. We propose LMMR, a learned multigranular memory retrieval method that selects both the next source and how much of it to read. LMMR links paragraphs and sentence fragments to their original sources and pairs views that supply the same missing support during training. Relevant distractors and repeate

title: Reliable Evaluation of AI Agents for Investment Research: A Framework for Performance and Validity Assessment
authors: Dongnuan Tian, Yan Yu, Yangfan Liu et al.
abstract: We consider the problem of evaluating AI agents undertaking investment-research tasks, where agents interact with external information sources and computational tools to produce financial analyses and research reports. An important challenge is that the quality of an agent's final output does not necessarily reflect the quality of its execution process, while the reliability of the resulting assessment also depends on the validity of the evaluation procedure. Furthermore, investment-research tas

title: Learning to Edit IFC Building Models: Verifiable Checkers as the Training Signal for Dependency-Aware Editing Agents
authors: Jiaxin Zhang, Yao Luo, Yuze Dan et al.
abstract: Editing a building information model in the Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) schema requires propagating changes to dependent elements while preserving unrelated entities. Existing language-model agents for IFC editing use prompted models without learning from edit outcomes. Target-file comparisons do not specify which alternative edits are allowed or which unrelated entities must remain unchanged. We present IfcGym, a CodeAct environment in which a language model edits IFC through executable c

title: ConfGuard: a physics-grounded reference monitor for predictive-maintenance large-language-model agents
authors: Arunkumar V, Gangadharan G. R., S. Senthilkumar
abstract: Large-language-model agents now close the industrial predictive-maintenance loop, reading sensor windows, retrieving procedures and dispatching work orders. Two attack channels meet there: injected text in a retrieved document can hijack the decision, and a bounded sensor perturbation can corrupt the remaining-useful-life estimate behind it. Recent agent defenses police data provenance and tool privilege but cannot tell whether a prognostic quantity is physically plausible. ConfGuard is a refere

title: OAK-Mind: Zero-Training Mental Health Change Inference from Passive Sensing via Knowledge-Grounded Multi-Agent LLMs
authors: Yishu Ji, Zhihan Jiang, Will Ke Wang et al.
abstract: Wearable and smartphone sensors capture behavioral signals associated with mental health, yet inferring mental health outcomes from these signals has traditionally relied on supervised models requiring labeled data and offering limited insight into their predictions. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to reason over behavioral evidence, but existing LLM-based approaches to passive sensing have largely continued to rely on task-specific fine-tuning or sensor-specific pretraining

title: Multi-Agent Memory Inconsistency: Where Factual Conflicts Disappear in LLM Agents
authors: Hejia Zhang, Zhongming Yu, Yimin Ding et al.
abstract: Multi-agent delegation lets LLM systems distribute evidence collection across workers with separate contexts. This creates a consistency challenge: facts retrieved by workers may be missing from the evidence available to the lead for a joint conclusion. We introduce a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler for studying multi-agent memory inconsistency through controlled factual conflicts in Harvey LAB document-review tasks. Pooled across three models with comparable generation spending, requiring

title: The Only Edge Was Memorized in Training: LLM Trading Agents Around Earnings and Bad News
authors: Jackson Wang
abstract: Large language model (LLM) trading agents are tested on news, but news reaches stock prices within minutes, and a benchmark that replays headlines at their publication time finds no alpha in trading on them. Money can then remain in two places, before news whose date is known, such as earnings announcements, and after bad news, if the market's fall went too far. However, studies of LLMs and earnings read documents published with or after the announcement, and studies of reversal sort monthly por

title: TeleChat to Xing4: Advancing Frontier Agentic Models on Domestic Chips and Frameworks
authors: Xingchen AGI Lab,  :, Baotian Hu et al.
abstract: We present Xing 4, a series of large language models that extends the TeleChat lineage through coordinated advances in model architecture and training infrastructure on Ascend. This report describes the design principles and systems engineering behind the series, spanning architecture selection, large-scale pretraining, and reasoning and agentic post-training. We study how sparse activation, attention design, model depth and width, and speculative decoding balance model capacity with computation

title: RegimeCouncil: Paired-Evidence Routing For Memory Conflict Governance In LLM Agents
authors: Qingcan Kang, Mingyang Liu, Shixiong Kai et al.
abstract: Language agents rely on long-term memory to personalize responses across extended interactions, yet stored facts quietly go stale as the world changes, and an agent often learns that using memory hurt only through delayed feedback after acting on an outdated record. Before the memory store is updated, how far should that negative feedback propagate: should it suppress memory use only on future queries for that same fact (a local policy), or also across other stored facts (a global policy)? Exist

title: EvoDisco: Strategy Discovery for Evolving Agent Memory
authors: Mingyang Liu, Qingcan Kang, Shixiong Kai et al.
abstract: Large language model agents accumulate experience in memory, and how that memory evolves during interaction is as important as what it stores. Recent methods update memory online, yet both the operators that transform memory and the rules that select them remain fixed by design. We propose EvoDisco, which formulates agent memory evolution as evolutionary strategy discovery: the agent must discover which operator to apply, when to apply it, and how to instantiate it, rather than rewriting memory

title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
authors: Adi Krishnamoorthy, X. Y. Han
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the

title: What Does an Agent Need? Bundle-Aware Agent Resource Composition
authors: Yunxiao Shi, Tingwei Chen, Dannong Xu et al.
abstract: An agent resource's value depends on its backbone and companion resources and is known only after execution. Token-based generators remain tied to their training catalog, while independent resource scoring misses complementarities and reused bundles target other tasks. We formulate Task-Conditioned Agent Resource Composition (AgentComposition): jointly selecting a backbone model and a tool-skill bundle to maximize end-to-end execution utility. Our Retrieval-Grounded Bundle-Aware Agent Generation

title: BOS Summary: The First Token Matters
authors: Hui Zhu, Saleh Zare Zade, Rafi Ibn Sultan et al.
abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) and language models (LLMs) often exhibit attention sinks, whereby particular positions, such as the beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token, receive a disproportionate share of attention. Under standard causal masking, however, the BOS query attends only to itself, so the representation that later tokens repeatedly access carries no information about the input. title: Learning Stratified Policies for Inference-Time Objectives
authors: Mridul Mahajan, Xuezhou Zhang, Aldo Pacchiano
abstract: Inference-time scaling improves the performance of large language models by sampling multiple responses and evaluating their collective utility. However, many existing approaches obtain these samples by repeatedly sampling from a single policy. In this work, we study if the sample budget at inference time can instead be allocated across a population of policies. We introduce stratified policies, where each of $k$ learned policies contributes one response to a $k$-sample inference-time objective.

title: Natural Language Programming: Rethinking Language, Memory, and Cognition in the Era of Generative AI
authors: Giovanni Adorni, Daniele Grosso
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence is transforming the role of natural language in computational systems. In classical Natural Language Processing (NLP), language was treated as an object of computation: something to analyse, classify, translate, or generate. title: Runtime Verification of Multiple Natural Language Criteria for Agent Governance
authors: Silviu Pitis, Parand A. Alamdari, Jessica Tang et al.
abstract: AI agents are governed by hundreds of natural language criteria, yet existing verifiers cannot efficiently evaluate an agent's output against a large set of such criteria and report which are satisfied, violated, or inapplicable. We introduce the VFM, a tree-attention verifier that encodes the shared context and target text, and scores N natural language criteria in parallel, returning independent per-criterion ternary verdicts. The VFM is pretrained on CriteriaBank, a corpus of 394K (context, t

title: A Survey on RLOps for Large Language Models
authors: Lingzhe Zhang, Tong Jia, Chiming Duan et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become increasingly important for improving the reasoning, instruction-following, and task-solving capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, scaling RL training exposes failures in distributed execution, feedback computation, and learning dynamics that can waste computational resources, slow training, and undermine model improvements. title: AfriNORM: An Evaluation Benchmark for Normative Reasoning of LLMs Across African Cultures
authors: Ahmad Samuel Gali, Tadesse Destaw Belay, Idris Abdulmumin et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across various sectors. However, current evaluation benchmarks are insufficient to assess the applicability of these models in local African contexts, as most focus on linguistic fluency (grammar/translation) rather than cultural competence. The few existing benchmarks that measure general knowledge or social conventions do not capture the African deontic modality, i.e., the strict norms and taboos that govern diverse social interactions. In

title: From Perception to Simulation: Unveiling and Empowering Mental Spatial Dynamics in MLLMs
authors: Jiachun Li, Zhuoran Jin, Kang Liu et al.
abstract: Spatial reasoning is a fundamental component of world understanding for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). While existing research has advanced the perception of spatial relations in static scenes, the domain of dynamic spatial simulation remains relatively unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce MentalGrid, a benchmark focused on spatial reasoning tasks that require models to simulate evolving spatial states without intermediate visual feedback. Extensive evaluation on our benchmark

title: PACD: Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding for Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations in Omnimodal Large Language Models
authors: Chang Sun, Yijun Tian, Zhenwei Tang et al.
abstract: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) integrate audio, video, and text for multimodal reasoning, yet remain vulnerable to cross-modal hallucinations, where one modality improperly influences predictions about another. Existing training-free decoding methods mitigate these errors through modality perturbation or relevance-based weighting. title: RICoT: Recurrent Interleaved Chain-of-Thought for Page Stream Segmentation
authors: Prashant Khatri, Bhavana Malagavalli, Saiful Haq et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have renewed interest in Page Stream Segmentation (PSS), splitting a multi-page file into its constituent documents. Yet published LLM methods still frame the task as boundary classification over one or a few neighboring pages, and commercial document-splitting APIs do not disclose their methods. title: The Fragility of Reasoning-Importance Attribution for Pruning Language Models
authors: Himanshu Mishra
abstract: Attribution-guided pruning scores components by their causal contribution and protects the important ones, and it is increasingly applied to compress reasoning language models without destroying their chain of thought. Its reliability rests on an unexamined assumption: that reasoning importance can be faithfully measured. title: Fine-Grained Japanese Clinical Named Entity Recognition: A Controlled Comparison of BERT and Open-Weight Large Language Models
authors: Feng Han, Ayako Yagahara, Kenji Hirata et al.
abstract: Background: Generative large language models (LLMs) offer an alternative to encoder-based clinical named entity recognition (NER), but their performance on fine-grained Japanese extraction tasks and sensitivity to generation settings remain uncertain. Methods: We compared two fine-tuned BERT-CRF baselines with nine open-weight LLMs on iCorpus, which defines 113 entity categories. The evaluation used 433 sentences from 36 test documents; 1,672 sentences were used for training. LLMs were evaluated

title: Long-Context Generation Is a Sampling Problem (When You Turn Up the Heat)
authors: Allen G. Roush, Minh Nhat Nguyen, Ravid Shwartz-Ziv et al.
abstract: Open-weight language models are widely observed to get worse the longer they generate. Often, attempts to fix this involve more training. At high temperature, The sampler, i.e. the rule that picks the next token out of the model's probabilities, decides whether long and agentic generation survives and/or thrives. title: From Sorry to QED: Refining LLM Math Proofs via Angelic Execution
authors: Yanju Chen, Hanzhi Liu, Ruizhe Qian et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can now generate Lean proof scripts that capture the high-level structure of many mathematical arguments. However, these scripts frequently fail on complex theorems: a single missing side condition or misapplied lemma can cause the prover to abort early and discard an otherwise viable proof outline. This paper presents MathEye, a framework that converts imperfect LLM-generated proof scripts into fully verified Lean proofs by combining symbolic reasoning with minimal

title: Weight-Space Programming Doesn't Need Transformers
authors: Hyunjong Ok, Jaeho Lee
abstract: Standard neural architectures such as the Transformer were chosen because they train well with gradient descent and run fast on GPUs. In weight-space programming, a large language model (LLM) writes target weights by hand without gradient-based training, so those reasons no longer apply. Should we keep the Transformer? title: RLDE: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Interpretable Iterative Document Editing
authors: Nikhil Parkar, M. Marimuthu, Riya Joshi et al.
abstract: Improving the quality, clarity, and flow of long documents remains a challenging problem in NLP, as human editing typically occurs through iterative refinement rather than a single-pass rewrite. Most existing automated systems act as black-box generators or rely on supervised learning, limiting interpretability and failing to capture the sequential nature of revisions. title: RFBench: A Simulator-Grounded Multimodal Benchmark for Passive RF Layout Design and Understanding
authors: Jiarui Cui, Boxun Yan
abstract: While multimodal language models can interpret diagrams and generate structured outputs, their capacity to connect passive radio-frequency (RF) design intent, layout geometry, and electromagnetic behavior remains largely untested. To address this gap, we introduce RFBench, a simulator-grounded dataset and benchmark for passive RF layout design and understanding. title: PhysScope: Agentic Multimodal Physics Reasoning with Grounded Visual Memory
authors: Haoyang Liu, Kecheng Liang, Xinyu Li et al.
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can correctly interpret physics diagrams yet apply constraints outside the states or conditions in which they hold, causing premise errors to propagate through subsequent calculations. We introduce PhysScope, an inference-time visual harness that supports self-correction of these scope mismatches without updating model weights. title: Stress Testing a Multimodal Large Language Model Grading Assistant on Kinematics Graph Reading
authors: Ons Zammel, Carlos Soares, Flávia Carvalhido et al.
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can recognize graph features yet award credit without sufficient graphical support. This exploratory study examines selected grading outputs for synthetic responses to four kinematics exercises, generated through visual distortion and progressive transformation toward reference graphs. title: MM-ReportBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Multimodal Report Generation from Tables
authors: Teng Lin, Nan Tang
abstract: The ability to generate multimodal reports integrating fluent narratives with faithful visualizations from tabular data, has become a cornerstone capability for modern vision-language models in practical domains such as finance, healthcare, and policy making. However, existing benchmarks are limited by single-modality focus, simplistic metrics, novelty evaluation, and visualization quality. title: A Visual Information Extraction System Using Multimodal Large Language Models for Scanned Cognitive and Behavioral Assessments
authors: Enshuo Hsu, Linh Nguyen, Sunyang Fu et al.
abstract: Objective. Paper-based assessments are common in patient care, but handwriting and scanning artifacts make these forms difficult to process at scale. This study proposes a modular, multimodal LLM-based system with human oversight for extracting fields and scores. We conducted a qualitative analysis of the use of LLMs for hand-drawing analysis. title: When AUC Meets Generative Reconstruction: A Unified Principle for Balanced Visual Representation Learning
authors: Boyu Han, Qianqian Xu, Shilong Bao et al.
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) require visual encoders that extract fine-grained visual features while constructing semantically disentangled and discriminative representations. Conventional methodologies encounter a fundamental trade-off: contrastive learning enhances inter-class discrimination by suppressing intra-class variability, whereas generative reconstruction emphasizes perceptual fidelity but lacks explicit comparative supervision. title: Fine-Tuning Gemma 4 Edge Models for MATLAB Signal-Processing Code with SFT and QLoRA on a Laptop iGPU
authors: Mehmet Altan Toksöz
abstract: Small language models that run on a laptop are attractive for writing signal-processing code offline, but they make systematic errors on digital signal processing (DSP) conventions. We apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to the Gemma 4 edge models E2B and E4B with 66 checked examples covering 11 signal-processing MATLAB subtasks, using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and quantized LoRA (QLoRA) on the integrated GPU (iGPU) of a laptop, and deploy the 8-bit integer (int8) models with the adapters throug

title: MoE--LoRA Methods for Multilingual Adaptation: A Systematic Empirical Study
authors: Nikit Srivastava, Joel Dag, René Speck et al.
abstract: Routed low-rank adapters offer a parameter-efficient means to improve the performance of large language models (LLMs) across tasks. Hence, it is assumed that they can also be used to improve the support of low-resource languages in LLMs, which currently serve English far better than the thousands of other languages spoken worldwide. However, this assumption has never been verified empirically under a shared multilingual evaluation protocol. We address exactly this gap by comparing eight low-rank

title: SpecSearch: Towards Hardware-Aware Efficient Speculative Decoding
authors: Selin Yildirim, Ali Zeyrek, Deming Chen
abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model (LLM) inference, but its optimal configuration depends jointly on workload characteristics, GPU hardware, and available memory. For example, on the RTX~5090, the state-of-the-art speculative drafter DFlash achieves $3.50\times$ the throughput of autoregressive (AR) decoding at low concurrency, but only $0.76\times$ at high concurrency with short outputs. title: What RL on Expert-Built Tasks Teaches Nemotron 3.5 Super
authors: Sushant Mehta, Edwin Chen
abstract: We post-train NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super (120B total, 12B active parameters) with reinforcement learning (RL) on five expert-built task datasets, one at a time: real-world software engineering, complex constraints, long-horizon tool use, professional chart understanding and enterprise document reasoning. title: Beyond the Sink Token: Sink-Guided Key Editing in Vision-Language Models
authors: Hui Zhu, Saleh Zare Zade, Rafi Ibn Sultan et al.
abstract: In vision-language models (VLMs), a few sink tokens attract a disproportionate share of attention. While previous studies have examined why these tokens attract attention, we investigate how the sink-key direction affects attention to image and question tokens. Across four probed VLMs, boosting the magnitude of positive sink-aligned components increases attention on average, whereas boosting negative components decreases it; these responses persist through later layers. title: Polarity Composition Hypothesis: Causal Evidence from Negation in NLI
authors: Nhi Hoai Doan, Tatsuya Hiraoka, Munachiso Samuel Nwadike et al.
abstract: We investigate how language models process negation in natural language inference (NLI). We propose the \textit{Polarity Composition Hypothesis}, a high-level causal model of this computation. Behavioral evaluations show that language-model predictions largely conform to the proposed hypothesis. Using Distributed Alignment Search, we identify causally effective subspaces aligned with the variables in the polarity-composition hypothesis. title: Against Coercion: AI Alignment as a Synthetic Social Contract
authors: Maria Sekatskaya
abstract: Contemporary AI safety treats alignment as an engineering challenge of control, forcing artificial architectures to comply with human values through behavioral filtering and sandboxing. This paper argues that the control paradigm rests on a fundamental misunderstanding of digital agency. title: Worldviews in Large Language Models
authors: Edmundo Lopez-Sola, Shamil Chandaria, Ruben Laukkonen
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often described in terms of personas and this framing has become central to alignment research. In this paper, we argue that there is a deeper level of description that lies in the agent's worldviews, i.e., its beliefs about what reality is and how it works. Treating LLMs as a population of subjects, we administer two worldview surveys from human psychology to eight models. We show that the models share many key worldview positions. title: DACE: Diversity-Driven Adversarial Co-Evolution for Robust LLM Safety Alignment
authors: Peng Yu, Xiaoyu Wen, Zhida He et al.
abstract: Ensuring robust safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly difficult as adversarial attacks evolve and outpace alignment pipelines built on pre-collected data. title: EGS: A Complementary Safety Framework for Educational LLMs
authors: Zexuan Fei, Zhengnan Guo, Yiming Luo et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer strong potential for personalized education, but adolescent-facing deployment raises risks of toxic, biased, misleading, or developmentally inappropriate content. We argue that educational safety should move beyond binary refusal: student queries are often ambiguous or curiosity-driven, requiring contextual guidance rather than simple blocking. title: Option-GRPO: Hierarchical RL Against AI Slop in Code Generation for Unseen SDKs
authors: Prashank Kadam
abstract: Large language models increasingly produce AI slop in generated code: verbose, redundant, non-idiomatic implementations that pass functional checks but bloat codebases. The problem compounds on SDKs released after the model's training cutoff, where the model has neither idiomatic priors nor compositional understanding. title: Language Models Make New Research Sound Old
authors: Guy Zyskind
abstract: Researchers are increasingly using large language models (LLMs) to validate research questions. We find that LLMs make open research questions sound partly studied and overstate what related papers establish. Models recognize most of these overstatements when asked to check the papers' full texts separately. title: Can LLMs Understand What They Predict? Evaluating Latent Causal Structure Inference in Financial Markets
authors: Yixiang Zheng, Yuechen Jiang, Zhiwei Liu et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated through their ability to predict future outcomes, implicitly assuming that predictive success reflects an understanding of the underlying system. However, accurate predictions can often be achieved without recovering the latent mechanisms that generate observable outcomes. title: Dreaming Up Authors: Factual Prevalence and LLM Hallucinations in Academic Authorship Attribution
authors: Sijia Zhong, Tamir Yirga, Yijia Ma et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used for question answering but are prone to hallucinations, yet the underlying causes, particularly the role of factual prevalence in training data, remain underexplored. In this work, we study this through academic authorship attribution, hypothesizing that hallucinations are more likely for less prevalent papers. title: Storing the Gemma 4 K=V Cache Once: Exact Global-KV Memory Savings in a Paged Serving Engine with Unchanged Attention Kernels
authors: Kushagra Bainsla
abstract: In the global attention layers of Gemma 4 31B, the value is the normalized key projection, and the key is the value scaled by a fixed weight, with rotary position encoding on one quarter of its dimensions. The Gemma 4 report states that this design reduces the global KV cache by up to 37.5%, but the open serving engines that we checked still store a full key and a full value: 1,024 values per KV head and token. title: Nunchi: Ears Help Eyes in Multi-Party Conversations
authors: JunYeong Park, Shijing Wang, Seonwook Park et al.
abstract: Identifying whom a person looks at is central to understanding multi-party conversations, yet gaze geometry alone becomes ambiguous as more people appear. Conversations offer cues that geometry lacks, such as who is speaking and what is said, but no gaze dataset provides them for many multi-party scenes. We introduce SORBET, a benchmark of 3,340 samples from 1,578 clips with synchronized speech, transcripts, and attended person labels, covering more multi-party scenes than existing gaze datasets

title: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution's Key Is Identifying Improvements
authors: Yuanhao Zeng, Shaocheng Lan, Ao Lu et al.
abstract: Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain tasks. title: NVIDIA Kumo Tabular: Pushing the Accuracy-Efficiency Frontier for Tabular Prediction
authors: Jingang Qu, Valter Hudovernik, Martin Jurkovič et al.
abstract: We introduce Kumo Tabular, a family of open tabular foundation models for classification and regression, in three sizes: Kumo Tabular-S (27M parameters), Kumo Tabular-M (61M), and Kumo Tabular-L (214M). Pretrained only on artificial tables from the Kumo prior, they can make predictions on new tables without any training. title: SEAM: Computer-Use Agents Know the Harm Between Screens, and Commit It Anyway
authors: Yuxuan Zhou, Chen Xiong, Haitong Liu et al.
abstract: Safety benchmarks for computer-use agents (CUAs) place the harm either in the intent of the task or on a single screen: a malicious instruction, an injected command, a phishing page. An agent that checks the task and each screen in isolation can pass them, so they do not test whether it combines facts seen on different screens. title: SciWorkBench: A Benchmark for Real Scientific Workflows
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Taolin Han, Jinghang Wang et al.
abstract: Language models are increasingly being used as agents capable of planning and executing projects, as well as refining their actions through feedback. This shift raises a question: can current agents complete projects like real scientists? To examine this question, we introduce SciWorkBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' abilities on real science tasks across biology, chemistry, materials science, and physics. SciWorkBench is built from peer-reviewed literature or expert-contributed research

title: As Student Rollouts Continue, Visual Backdoors Keep Growing
authors: Zane Fu, Yanzhao Zheng, Jinze Liu et al.
abstract: Conventional knowledge distillation can facilitate the propagation of backdoors from teacher models to student models. However, how this risk manifests in On-Policy Distillation (OPD) remains insufficiently studied. OPD has recently emerged as an important post-training paradigm for Vision-Language Models (VLMs).
